(2) For each test protein, create a conditional target as in the chosen diffusion baseline (e.g., function/family label if available in their standard dataset; if not, use unconditional generation but match length distribution). (3) Models: Baseline A: a sequence-only diffusion generator from the multi-level conditional diffusion paper (ablation: remove structure/all-atom tracks). Model B: the full multi-level conditional diffusion model, or if open weights are unavailable, substitute the most complete open-weight structure+sequence generator available from the provided papers and keep Baseline A as its sequence-only ablation. (4) For each generated sequence, predict structure with an open model (e.g., ESMFold) and compute its molecular surface (e.g., solvent-accessible surface area per residue and surface point cloud via an open tool like FreeSASA/MSMS-equivalent). (5) Failure-mode/ablation diagnostic: within Model B, ablate the highest-level representation (all-atom or backbone track) while keeping sequence diffusion identical, and measure surface degradation.
decisive_metric: Surface-conditioned distributional agreement measured as (i) MMD between generated vs real distributions of per-residue solvent accessibility profiles (SASA vector statistics) and (ii) binding-site proxy consistency: KL/MMD between distributions of hydrophobic-patch size on the surface (connected components of high hydrophobicity on exposed residues). Report both overall and stratified by length bin; the mechanism is supported specifically if multi-level/all-atom reduces these surface-distribution distances compared to sequence-only, and the ablation increases them.
supporting_result: Compared to the sequence-only baseline, the multi-level/all-atom model shows a clear, statistically significant reduction in surface-profile MMD (e.g., >15% relative drop with bootstrap CI excluding 0) and hydrophobic-patch distribution distance, and the all-atom/backbone ablation reverses most of this gain while leaving simple sequence-level diversity/novelty roughly unchanged.
falsifying_result: Surface-profile MMD and hydrophobic-patch distribution distances are indistinguishable between multi-level/all-atom and sequence-only (or worsen), and the all-atom/backbone ablation does not materially change surface metrics; this would indicate the claimed reliability improvements are not mediated by better surface-level geometry and makes surface-aware extensions/evaluations less compelling as a next step.

literature_gap: Multiple papers propose alternative guidance rules to avoid CFG pathologies (CFG++ attributes mode collapse and non-invertibility to off-manifold steps; APG attributes oversaturation/artifacts to the component of the CFG update parallel to the conditional prediction). However, No Training, No Problem proposes guidance that does not rely on an unconditional/marginal model (ICG) and even applies to unconditional models (TSG). It is unclear whether the key CFG pathologies are fundamentally driven by off-manifold/parallel-component geometry (as in CFG++/APG) or by dependence on a separately learned marginal/unconditional branch (which ICG/TSG claim to remove). There is no direct, mechanism-level evaluation comparing whether training-free guidance also reduces off-manifold drift and improves invertibility, or whether it simply trades one failure mode for another.
hypothesis: If CFG’s main pathologies (invertibility failure and high-scale artifacts) are primarily caused by off-manifold drift from the guidance update geometry rather than by the need for an explicit unconditional/marginal model, then replacing standard CFG with geometry-constrained guidance (CFG++ or APG) should improve round-trip invertibility and reduce off-manifold drift more than training-free guidance (ICG/TSG) on the same pretrained model, even when all methods are matched for prompt adherence.
minimal_test: Use one open-weight text-to-image diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion v1.5) and run a tiny image-editing round-trip test that directly probes invertibility. Pick 200 COCO captions (public) and for each caption generate an image x0 with each method at a fixed sampler (DDIM, 50 steps): (A) standard CFG baseline, (B) CFG++ (from its paper), (C) APG (from its paper), (D) ICG (from No Training, No Problem) applied at inference, and optionally (E) TSG as an unconditional control by using empty prompt or unconditional sampling. Then perform an edit-and-invert cycle: forward diffuse x0 to noise at timestep T, then reconstruct x0_hat by running the corresponding reverse sampler using the same prompt and method; additionally perform a mild prompt edit (e.g., append a single attribute like color) and measure whether inversion to the original prompt recovers x0. Keep guidance scales tuned per method to match a target CLIP-text similarity band (so comparisons are not confounded by different adherence). Total compute fits in <=8 A100 GPU-days.
decisive_metric: Round-trip invertibility error decomposed into (1) pixel/LPIPS distance between x0 and x0_hat for same-prompt cycle, and (2) latent trajectory off-manifold drift proxy: average norm of the update component orthogonal to the model’s conditional score direction across timesteps (the orthogonal/parallel decomposition used by APG), plus (3) saturation/artifact score: mean saturation in HSV and fraction of pixels clipped near 0/1. Report curves vs guidance scale for each method under the prompt-adherence-matched constraint.
supporting_result: Under matched prompt adherence, CFG++ and/or APG show substantially lower LPIPS round-trip error and lower orthogonal drift proxy than standard CFG, while ICG/TSG do not improve (or improve less) on these mechanism metrics; additionally, CFG++/APG reduce saturation/clipping at high guidance scales relative to CFG, consistent with geometry/off-manifold explanations.
falsifying_result: ICG or TSG achieves equal or better round-trip invertibility (lower LPIPS error) and equal or lower off-manifold drift proxy than CFG++/APG under matched prompt adherence, or none of the methods (CFG++/APG/ICG/TSG) meaningfully improves invertibility/drift relative to standard CFG despite reducing saturation. Either outcome would weaken the claim that geometry-constrained guidance is the decisive fix for CFG pathologies in this setting and make the proposed direction less compelling.

literature_gap: There is a cross-paper mechanism/evaluation mismatch: Phase-PGF and MovingParts claim phase- or motion-factorized representations enable macro-motion analysis/part discovery in dynamic scenes, but the open-vocabulary text-to-motion method (Textual Decomposition then Sub-motion-space Scattering) targets compositional generalization without any grounded test that its atomic-motion decomposition corresponds to physically coherent, reusable motion factors. Conversely, the dynamic-scene papers do not test whether their discovered motion factors are compositional primitives that could align with language-level “atomic motions”. The neighborhood lacks a minimal test of whether motion factors extracted from real dynamic scenes behave like reusable atomic actions (i.e., stable under recomposition) rather than dataset-specific latent codes.
hypothesis: If motion-factorized representations from MovingParts (part-level rigid motions) are true reusable motion primitives, then re-composing them to satisfy a novel text prompt built from atomic actions (as in Textual Decomposition) should preserve physical/kinematic coherence better than directly generating the full motion with a text-to-motion baseline, because factorization constrains motions to consistent part trajectories.
minimal_test: Use a public text-to-motion dataset with 3D joints (e.g., HumanML3D) and an open-weight text-to-motion generator baseline corresponding to the Textual Decomposition then Sub-motion-space Scattering approach (or its released implementation). Construct 50 compositional prompts by concatenating 2-3 atomic actions (e.g., “raise right arm then turn left then sit”). For each prompt: (1) Baseline: generate motion directly from the text-to-motion model. (2) Factorized-recompose test: take a small set of real motions containing the atomic actions, extract part-level rigid motion factors with MovingParts-style motion factorization (applied to joint trajectories by clustering joints with similar rigid transforms across time; an ablation is to randomize the grouping), then recompose factors in the prompt order with simple temporal blending (as in DIP-style blending). Keep duration matched. Evaluate physical plausibility and action-order correctness. Resource: 1-2 days to implement factor extraction/recomposition and run 100 generations; <=8 A100 GPU-days for generation and any lightweight fitting.
decisive_metric: Two diagnostics: (1) Kinematic physicality: foot-skate ratio and ground-penetration rate computed from joint trajectories (per-frame foot velocity when foot is in contact; and fraction of frames with ankle below estimated ground plane). (2) Compositional action fidelity: a pretrained open-weight motion-text retrieval model (e.g., CLIP-style for motion) used to compute per-atomic-action segment retrieval accuracy: whether each generated segment is closest to the corresponding atomic text among distractors, and whether the temporal order matches (segment-level top-1 accuracy across the sequence). Include an ablation diagnostic: compare correct factor grouping vs randomized joint grouping for recomposition.
supporting_result: Recomposition using MovingParts-style factors yields meaningfully lower foot-skate and penetration (e.g., >=20% relative reduction) while maintaining or improving segment-level atomic-action retrieval accuracy and correct action order compared to direct baseline generation. Additionally, randomized grouping substantially degrades these metrics, indicating the gain comes from meaningful motion factorization rather than just blending.
falsifying_result: Recomposition does not improve (or worsens) physicality metrics (foot-skate/penetration) and/or significantly reduces segment-level atomic-action retrieval/order accuracy versus the direct text-to-motion baseline, and randomized grouping performs similarly to the “correct” factor grouping. This would suggest the discovered motion factors are not reusable atomic primitives for compositional open-vocabulary motion generation, making the direction not worth pursuing under this mechanism claim.

literature_gap: WeLore argues low-rank structure emerges non-uniformly across layers and should be compressed with layer-wise rank allocation driven by singular value heavy-tails, while Lily claims cross-layer interconnected low-rank adapters can break the low-rank update constraint and improve adaptation under the same parameter budget. It is unclear (and untested across these works) whether cross-layer coupling is actually needed once ranks are allocated non-uniformly per layer based on measured low-rankness, or whether the gains come mainly from effectively reallocating rank/expressivity across layers.
hypothesis: If Lily’s gains primarily come from cross-layer coupling (not just better rank allocation), then with the same adapter parameter budget, Lily should yield higher effective update rank in layer space and better downstream performance than a WeLore-style non-uniform per-layer LoRA that matches Lily’s per-layer parameter allocation, because cross-layer shared projectors create higher-rank, more diverse update subspaces across layers.
minimal_test: Use an open LLM (e.g., Llama-2-7B or Mistral-7B open weights) and one public instruction/QA tuning task (e.g., Alpaca-clean subset or OpenAssistant small subset) for a short fine-tune (e.g., 2k-10k steps). Compare two PEFT methods at equal total trainable parameters: (A) Lily (as described) and (B) a control that removes cross-layer coupling but keeps WeLore-motivated non-uniform ranks: per-layer LoRA ranks chosen by a one-shot SVD heavy-tail criterion on the base weights (proxying WeLore’s rank reduction ratio) and then scaled so total parameters match Lily. Include an ablation diagnostic: Lily with cross-layer connections disabled (independent HP per layer or no shared HP), keeping parameter count fixed. Keep optimizer, data, and training compute identical; run 2 seeds.
decisive_metric: Mechanism metric: effective rank of the realized weight update per layer and across layers, measured by the spectrum of DeltaW after training (e.g., stable rank = (||DeltaW||_F^2)/(||DeltaW||_2^2)) and the cross-layer diversity of update subspaces (e.g., mean pairwise principal angle or CKA between per-layer DeltaW low-rank factors). Outcome metric: task performance (validation loss / exact match or accuracy) reported secondarily, but decision hinges on whether Lily increases effective update rank/diversity beyond the matched non-uniform per-layer LoRA control.
supporting_result: At matched parameter budget, Lily shows consistently higher stable rank of DeltaW in multiple mid/upper layers and higher cross-layer subspace diversity than the non-uniform per-layer LoRA control and the 'Lily-without-coupling' ablation, and this coincides with a meaningful validation improvement (e.g., lower loss and/or higher accuracy) over both controls across seeds.
falsifying_result: When parameter budgets are matched, Lily’s effective DeltaW stable-rank and cross-layer subspace diversity are similar to (or lower than) the non-uniform per-layer LoRA control, and performance differences are negligible or favor the control; additionally, disabling Lily’s cross-layer coupling does not materially reduce rank/diversity or performance. This would indicate cross-layer coupling is not the key mechanism beyond rank allocation, making the direction less worth pursuing.

literature_gap: SALMONN-omni claims a codec-free full-duplex design with a special "thinking" step to align text/audio rates, while EMOVA attributes gains to a semantic-acoustic disentangled speech tokenizer for omni-modal alignment. Across these papers, it is unclear whether (and how much) full-duplex robustness to self-generated speech/background interference depends on disentangling semantic vs acoustic/style information versus architectural streaming tricks (e.g., the thinking step). This mechanism is also highlighted as a key evaluation gap by the roadmap paper emphasizing paralinguistic/abstract acoustic knowledge handling.
hypothesis: If self-interference failures in full-duplex speech LLMs are driven by entanglement between semantic content and acoustic/style cues, then replacing a baseline entangled tokenizer with a semantic-acoustic disentangled tokenizer (EMOVA-style) will reduce semantic errors under self-play overlap because the model can better ignore non-semantic acoustic variations while decoding meaning.
minimal_test: Using open-weight components only, construct a minimal full-duplex self-interference evaluation on a public ASR set (e.g., LibriSpeech test-clean): take each utterance x(t) and create an overlapped version x_mix(t)=x(t)+alpha*y(t-lag) where y is the model's own generated speech from the previous turn (self-play) and lag is 0-500 ms; run two systems under identical training budget: (A) SALMONN-style audio-to-LLM with a standard single-stream speech tokenizer/codec (entangled) and (B) the same model but swapping in a semantic-acoustic disentangled speech tokenizer plus the lightweight style module disabled (to isolate disentanglement). Keep the "thinking" step on for both to control for streaming alignment. Evaluate only inference and light adapter-tuning if needed within <=8 A100 GPU-days. Include one ablation diagnostic: remove disentanglement by shuffling acoustic tokens across examples while keeping semantic tokens fixed during adapter-tuning, to test whether improvements rely on the separation.
decisive_metric: Delta WER as a function of overlap severity: WER(x_mix) minus WER(x) plotted versus alpha and lag, plus a targeted diagnostic on paralinguistic leakage: rate of lexical substitutions correlated with pitch/energy changes in y (measured by correlating per-utterance F0/energy of y with WER increase).
supporting_result: System B shows a consistently smaller WER increase than A across alpha/lag (e.g., >=10-20% relative reduction in WER degradation at moderate overlap) and the correlation between y's F0/energy and WER degradation is substantially reduced in B; the shuffling ablation removes most of B's gain, indicating the mechanism is the semantic/acoustic separation rather than extra capacity.
falsifying_result: System B matches A within noise on WER degradation across overlap conditions, or improves only when style capacity is enabled but not when isolating disentanglement; additionally, the shuffling ablation does not reduce B's advantage (or B has no advantage), implying disentanglement is not the driver and the direction is not worth pursuing for full-duplex robustness.

literature_gap: Feature Discrimination Analysis claims ultra-low-bit quantization can improve class separability despite high quantization error, while CBQ argues ultra-low-bit PTQ failure in LLMs is driven by intensified inter/intra-layer dependencies that harm accuracy (not just error magnitude). It is unclear whether any measurable representation-level “discrimination” gain from low-bit quantization exists in LLMs, or whether LLM degradation is dominated by cross-layer dependency breakage so that discrimination cannot improve without cross-block reconstruction.
hypothesis: If CBQ’s cross-block reconstruction is addressing a dependency-driven failure mode (not merely reducing per-layer quantization error), then compared to a layer-wise PTQ baseline at the same bit-width, CBQ should better preserve (or increase) representation discrimination between semantically different inputs across layers, and this preservation should be concentrated at layers where cross-block dependencies are strongest.
minimal_test: Quantize an open LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B or Llama-2-7B) to W4A4 using (a) a standard layer-wise/block-wise PTQ baseline from CBQ’s compared methods (or the simplest layer-wise reconstruction baseline described in CBQ) and (b) CBQ. Use a small public calibration set (e.g., WikiText-2 train subset) and evaluate on a public contrastive discrimination probe built from sentence pairs (e.g., STS-B or MRPC from GLUE). For each model (FP16, baseline PTQ, CBQ), extract hidden states at several depths for each sentence and compute discrimination as the separation between matched pairs vs mismatched pairs (same-pair cosine similarity minus different-pair cosine similarity), then relate this to downstream generation quality on a small public eval (e.g., WikiText-2 perplexity) as a sanity check. Include an ablation diagnostic: run CBQ but disable cross-block dependency modeling (keep only intra-layer rounding / per-block reconstruction) to isolate the cross-block mechanism.
decisive_metric: Layer-wise discrimination gap delta: for each layer l, DeltaDisc(l) = [mean cosine(h_l(s1), h_l(s2)) for true pairs] - [mean cosine(h_l(s1), h_l(s2')) for mismatched pairs], and the change vs FP16 (or vs baseline PTQ). Key diagnostic is whether CBQ restores DeltaDisc(l) relative to the baseline PTQ specifically at mid/deep layers, and whether the cross-block-disabled ablation loses that restoration.
supporting_result: At W4A4, baseline layer-wise PTQ shows a clear collapse of DeltaDisc(l) (especially mid/deep layers) versus FP16, while CBQ significantly restores DeltaDisc(l) toward FP16 (or exceeds it slightly) at those layers; the CBQ cross-block-disabled ablation fails to restore DeltaDisc(l) to the same extent. The degree of DeltaDisc restoration correlates with improved WikiText-2 perplexity relative to baseline PTQ.
falsifying_result: CBQ does not improve DeltaDisc(l) relative to the baseline PTQ at the same bit-width (improvements are negligible, inconsistent across layers, or not concentrated where dependencies are expected), or the cross-block-disabled ablation matches CBQ on DeltaDisc(l). In this case, the proposed mechanism-level link between cross-block dependency handling and representation discrimination is not supported, weakening the direction of using discrimination-based analysis/targets for LLM ultra-low-bit PTQ.

literature_gap: SemSA claims head-specific semantic sparse masks preserve accuracy with large speedups, but it is unclear whether those masks preserve the specific multi-head communication features and reusable circuits highlighted by circuit-tracing work (Sparse Attention Decomposition Applied to Circuit Tracing; Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks). There is a cross-paper tension between efficiency-driven head sparsification and mechanism preservation: SemSA evaluates task accuracy/latency, while the circuit papers emphasize specific heads and inter-head signal paths that may be fragile to mask changes even when aggregate accuracy looks unchanged.
hypothesis: If SemSA-style per-head sparse masks truly preserve the semantics of important attention heads, then applying those masks to the known IOI circuit heads should preserve circuit-level causal effects (patching/ablation signatures) because the key sparse-coded communication features in head matrices are still reachable through the retained attention links.
minimal_test: Use an open-weight GPT-2 Small (as in the circuit-tracing paper) on the IOI dataset. Implement inference-time attention masking in the style of SemSA: for each head, keep the top-k attention links per query token (choose k to match a target sparsity level, e.g., 50% and 80% attention sparsity), leaving values/weights unchanged. Baselines/controls: (1) dense attention (no mask); (2) uniform sparse mask with the same overall sparsity applied identically to all heads (SemSA’s contrasted baseline). Diagnostic ablation: perform causal head ablations on the canonical IOI circuit head set versus non-circuit heads (use the IOI head list from Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks, or the standard IOI circuit head set they reproduce) under each masking condition. Measure whether circuit heads remain uniquely necessary under SemSA-style masking.
decisive_metric: Causal effect preservation of the IOI circuit under sparsity: for each condition, compute (a) IOI accuracy drop when ablating the circuit heads minus accuracy drop when ablating an equal-number size-matched random head set (delta-necessity), and (b) correlation of per-head ablation impacts between dense and sparse settings (Spearman over heads). These directly test whether the same heads and pathways remain causally important rather than only whether overall accuracy is high.
supporting_result: Under SemSA-style head-specific masks, IOI accuracy remains near dense, and the delta-necessity remains close to dense (circuit-head ablation hurts much more than random-head ablation), with high correlation of per-head ablation impacts vs dense (e.g., Spearman >= 0.8). Uniform sparsity at the same level shows a larger degradation of delta-necessity and/or lower correlation, indicating SemSA better preserves the circuit mechanism.
falsifying_result: Even when IOI accuracy is maintained, SemSA-style masking substantially reduces or reshuffles causal head importance: circuit-head ablation no longer produces a much larger drop than random-head ablation (delta-necessity collapses toward 0), and/or per-head ablation impacts have low correlation with dense (e.g., Spearman <= 0.3). This would suggest SemSA-like sparsification does not preserve the mechanistic circuit communication claimed by circuit-tracing/reuse results, weakening the case that semantic sparse masks are mechanism-faithful rather than merely accuracy-preserving.

literature_gap: APO argues Nesterov-style momentum accelerates iterative preference optimization by viewing it as a proximal point method, but AIPO shows iterative DPO pipelines can amplify a specific failure mode (length exploitation) across iterations. It is unresolved whether momentum-based acceleration worsens this iteration-induced distributional pathology (longer responses) even when aggregate win-rate improves, i.e., an optimization-speed vs preference-miscalibration/length-exploitation tension.
hypothesis: If we add Nesterov-style momentum (APO-style) to an iterative DPO self-training pipeline, length exploitation will increase relative to non-momentum iterative DPO because momentum amplifies step-to-step drift from the human-preference length distribution under synthetic preference noise, even when preference loss decreases faster.
minimal_test: Using an open-weight instruction model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct or Mistral-7B-Instruct) and a public preference dataset (UltraFeedback or HH-RLHF), run a 2-iteration self-training pipeline with identical data, hyperparameters, and stopping criteria across conditions: (A) iterative DPO baseline (as in AIPO) and (B) APO-style momentum iterative preference optimization (momentum on policy updates as in APO). Keep the same reference model and same synthetic preference generation procedure between A and B. Evaluate after each iteration on a fixed held-out prompt set (e.g., MT-Bench prompts or a held-out subset of UltraFeedback prompts). Include one ablation diagnostic: momentum on vs off while matching the final training loss (early stop B to match A’s training loss) to separate speed effects from endpoint effects.
decisive_metric: Length exploitation slope across iterations: change in response length distribution relative to a human/reference distribution, measured as (i) delta in median token length per iteration and (ii) KL divergence between model response-length histogram and the human-chosen response-length histogram from the preference dataset, tracked over iterations. Secondary check: preference calibration vs length by computing win-rate in pairs after length-matching (truncate both responses to same token budget) to see if gains disappear when length is controlled.
supporting_result: Compared to iterative DPO, the momentum condition shows a significantly larger positive slope in median length and larger increase in length-distribution KL across iterations, while its apparent win-rate gains substantially shrink or vanish under length-matched evaluation; the loss-matched ablation still shows higher length drift under momentum.
falsifying_result: Momentum does not increase length exploitation: the momentum condition’s length slope and length-distribution KL across iterations are comparable to or lower than iterative DPO, and any win-rate gains persist under length-matched evaluation; additionally, when loss-matched, momentum no longer shows extra length drift.

literature_gap: There is a tension between (1) LLM-based multi-agent simulation frameworks that claim scalable inter-agent interaction but are not evaluated on explicit agent-to-agent coordination (Very Large-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation with LLM-Powered Agents limitation), and (2) evidence that LLMs fail on true multi-agent planning/coordination problems like MAPF beyond trivial settings (Why Solving MAPF with LLMs has not Succeeded Yet). It is unclear whether adding an explicit, constrained communication/control structure (e.g., FSM-style coordination as in MetaAgent) actually fixes the coordination failure mode, or whether the limitation is primarily planning/search rather than communication.
hypothesis: If we impose an explicit finite-state communication protocol for an LLM-based multi-agent controller on MAPF, then collision-free coordination success should increase because the FSM constrains messaging and action choices into consistent, traceable coordination phases (negotiation, reservation, move/hold), reducing inconsistent or mutually incompatible agent plans that cause deadlocks/collisions.
minimal_test: Run a small MAPF evaluation with open-weight LLM agents (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or similar) on standard grid MAPF instances with obstacles (the setting where the MAPF paper reports failure). Compare two conditions with identical prompts, model, and per-step token budget: (A) unconstrained chat-based multi-agent planning (baseline aligned with the MAPF LLM approach), vs (B) the same LLM wrapped by a minimal FSM controller inspired by MetaAgent with 3-4 states (Propose path segment, Broadcast intent, Resolve conflicts/assign priorities, Execute next move). Use a simple environment runner that steps the grid world and enforces collision rules. Include one ablation/diagnostic: in condition (B) disable the Resolve conflicts state (skip directly from Broadcast to Execute) to test whether the hypothesized mechanism is specifically conflict resolution rather than just structured prompting.
decisive_metric: Conflict-resolution effectiveness: (1) collision rate per 100 environment steps and (2) deadlock rate (fraction of episodes where no agent reaches its goal progress for K consecutive steps, e.g., K=10) measured separately from overall success. These directly test whether structured inter-agent coordination reduces the coordination failure modes reported for LLM MAPF.
supporting_result: Compared to (A), condition (B) shows a large reduction in collision rate and deadlock rate (e.g., >30% relative reduction in each) at similar step/token budgets, and the ablation that removes the Resolve conflicts state substantially worsens these rates toward (A), indicating the gain is specifically from explicit conflict-resolution coordination.
falsifying_result: Condition (B) does not materially reduce collision or deadlock rates versus (A) (e.g., differences within noise or <10% relative), or any apparent improvement remains even when the Resolve conflicts state is removed (ablation matches (B)), implying the FSM structure/communication protocol is not addressing the core MAPF failure mode and the direction is unlikely to be worth pursuing.

literature_gap: Training-free attention/gradient-based cropping claims MLLMs already know where to look for small details (DgaY5mDdmT), but encoder-focused work argues fine-grained perception hinges on accessing shallow/multi-level visual features (syoLhUJmth) and that visual recognition errors bottleneck downstream reasoning (6zAIFLgayn). It is unclear whether cropping improves answers by truly improving fine-grained visual perception (recovering the missing visual signal) versus merely acting as a prompt-time cue that helps the LLM guess; and the cropping paper’s baseline is weak (no fair comparison), leaving a cross-paper mechanism/evaluation mismatch.
hypothesis: If training-free cropping helps because it restores missing fine-grained visual evidence (not just prompt-time bias), then after cropping the model’s token-level confidence should become more sensitive to the correct local visual evidence and less sensitive to language priors on low-level questions, because the relevant pixels are now resolvable by the vision encoder.
minimal_test: Use Q-Bench LLVisionQA (0V5TVt9bk0) as the low-level perception target. Pick one open-weight MLLM used in the cropping paper (DgaY5mDdmT) or a comparable open-weight model. Run three inference conditions on the same questions: (1) No crop (baseline from DgaY5mDdmT), (2) Attention/gradient-based crop as in DgaY5mDdmT (training-free), (3) Random crop control matched in size/aspect ratio and centered on a random location (failure-mode control). Additionally, add a language-prior stress test by shuffling answer options or replacing the question text with a templated neutral version that preserves the asked attribute but removes strong priors (e.g., remove object names if present) while keeping the image unchanged. Compute all metrics without any model training (fits <=8 A100 GPU-days).
decisive_metric: Evidence-sensitivity diagnostic: the change in image dependence measured by (a) the drop in accuracy when the image is replaced by a blank/noise image (image-ablation gap) and (b) the change in calibrated log-prob margin between correct vs best incorrect option under image perturbations localized to the predicted crop region versus outside it (region perturbation test). The key quantity is whether cropping increases the image-ablation gap and region-local perturbation sensitivity relative to both no-crop and random-crop, indicating the model is using recovered visual evidence rather than priors.
supporting_result: Compared to no-crop and random-crop, attention/gradient cropping yields (1) higher LLVisionQA accuracy, and (2) a substantially larger image-ablation gap and stronger region-local perturbation sensitivity (correct-vs-incorrect log-prob margin collapses when perturbing inside the crop but not when perturbing an equal-area outside region). The language-prior stress test shows smaller degradation under question neutralization for the cropped condition than for no-crop, implying reduced reliance on priors due to improved visual evidence.
falsifying_result: Cropping improves (or matches) accuracy but does not increase image-ablation gap or region-local perturbation sensitivity relative to no-crop, or performs similarly to random-crop; and/or under language-prior stress (question neutralization/shuffled options) the cropped condition degrades as much as or more than no-crop. This pattern would indicate the gain is not from restored fine-grained perception and makes the training-free cropping direction less worth pursuing as a perception mechanism.

literature_gap: ECL claims empowerment-driven exploration plus causal-structure learning improves controllability and task learning, but it does not directly test whether the learned causal structure is actually better (or more robust) under realistic assumption violations. This conflicts with the broader causal-discovery evidence that differentiable methods can appear robust under SHD/SID except under scale variation; empowerment exploration could also induce scale variation or non-i.i.d. data that breaks structure learning, undermining the claimed mechanism.
hypothesis: If empowerment-driven exploration truly facilitates causal reasoning in model-based RL (as in ECL), then compared to non-empowerment exploration it should improve causal graph quality under the same data budget, because empowerment visits interventions/trajectories that better identify causal parents; however, if empowerment mostly changes variable scales/coverage in ways known to harm differentiable causal discovery, graph quality will not improve and may degrade particularly under scale variation.
minimal_test: On a small public synthetic control environment with known ground-truth causal graph and continuous state (e.g., a simple SCM-based dynamics simulator used in causal discovery benchmarks), collect two fixed-size datasets of transitions (same number of environment steps): (A) ECL-style empowerment-maximizing exploration using a causal dynamics model, and (B) a baseline exploration without empowerment (e.g., random or curiosity-only as in ECL ablation). For each dataset, run one differentiable causal discovery method benchmarked in the robustness paper (baseline) to infer the graph. Add one explicit misspecification condition by rescaling a subset of state dimensions by large factors during data collection (scale-variation setting) while keeping the underlying causal graph unchanged. Total runs: 2 exploration modes x 2 scale settings, with 3 random seeds.
decisive_metric: Change in Structural Intervention Distance (SID) of the inferred graph relative to ground truth between (A) and (B), reported separately for normal-scale and scale-variation settings; plus a diagnostic plot of per-variable empirical standard deviation ratios (max/min) to confirm whether empowerment increases scale variation in the collected dataset.
supporting_result: With normal scaling, empowerment exploration yields consistently lower SID than the non-empowerment baseline at the same step budget; under scale variation, empowerment does not worsen SID relative to baseline (or improves it), and the scale diagnostic shows empowerment does not induce substantially higher variance ratios than baseline (or remains robust despite them).
falsifying_result: Empowerment exploration shows no SID improvement over baseline (difference within noise) or higher SID in the normal setting, and/or under scale variation empowerment leads to markedly worse SID than baseline while also exhibiting larger variance-ratio diagnostics, indicating the claimed empowerment->better causal structure mechanism is not reliable and may be counterproductive under a known failure mode.

literature_gap: HowToCaption claims LLM-rewritten, temporally aligned captions from noisy ASR improve text-video retrieval, while CrossTVR’s gains come from fine-grained cross-attention re-ranking over frozen CLIP tokens; it is unclear whether caption “cleaning” actually improves true visual grounding (as opposed to exploiting language priors) in a setting that explicitly provides ASR and evaluates grounding beyond single-sentence captions (Video-CSR). No cross-paper check isolates whether improved retrieval comes from reduced ASR noise vs increased hallucinated/biased text that a cross-attention re-ranker can overfit.
hypothesis: If HowToCaption-style LLM rewriting reduces supervision noise and increases visual grounding (not just fluency), then training a standard dual-encoder retriever on rewritten captions should yield larger gains on Video-CSR retrieval when queries are ASR-debiased (visual-only) than when queries are ASR-heavy, because the mechanism is better text-video alignment to visuals rather than better language matching to speech.
minimal_test: Train the same open-weight text-video dual-encoder baseline twice on a small public subset of HowTo100M: (A) original ASR subtitle segments as text, (B) HowToCaption-rewritten captions for the same segments (use the released HowToCaption). Then evaluate on Video-CSR retrieval (caption-based and summary-excerpt-based) under two query variants: (1) original human caption/summary excerpt, (2) an ASR-masked version where all tokens overlapping with the video’s ASR transcript (string match with stemming) are removed from the query. Add CrossTVR re-ranker (open CLIP backbone) as a second-stage on top of each trained retriever to see whether any gains are amplified only after cross-attention. Compute within the 8 A100 GPU-day budget by limiting training to e.g., 200k pairs and evaluating on full Video-CSR.
decisive_metric: Delta in Recall@K (K=1,5,10) between (B) and (A) specifically on the ASR-masked query condition, plus a diagnostic “ASR-overlap sensitivity” curve: performance as a function of the fraction of query tokens removed (bucketed), reported separately with and without CrossTVR re-ranking. This directly tests whether gains persist when speech-correlated tokens are removed and whether CrossTVR is merely exploiting language overlap.
supporting_result: HowToCaption training (B) improves Recall@K over ASR training (A) by a larger margin in the ASR-masked condition than in the original-query condition (e.g., +3-5 R@10 masked vs +0-1 R@10 unmasked), and the improvement remains without CrossTVR (or is only modestly amplified by CrossTVR), indicating better visual grounding rather than just better language matching.
falsifying_result: HowToCaption’s advantage appears only (or mainly) in the unmasked condition and collapses to ~0 or negative in the ASR-masked condition, and/or gains emerge only after adding CrossTVR re-ranking (suggesting the rewritten captions mainly add exploitable language regularities rather than improving visual alignment). This would weaken the case that caption rewriting is a worthwhile path for grounded retrieval.

literature_gap: RAG-SR motivates retrieval to mitigate LLM hallucinations by grounding generation in previously searched symbolic expressions, while ChatSR claims natural-language instructions can reliably steer expression generation to satisfy symbol/structure requirements. Neither establishes whether retrieval actually improves constraint satisfaction under instruction, or whether it instead anchors the model to retrieved candidates and hurts instruction-following, especially on out-of-distribution symbol/operator demands highlighted by ChatSR's limited symbol types. This is a mechanism-level tension: retrieval-grounding vs instruction-steering for controllable symbolic regression.
hypothesis: If we add retrieval of top-K previously evaluated expressions into an instruction-following SR generator, constraint satisfaction (e.g., must include sin and be periodic) should increase without degrading fit, because retrieval reduces hallucinated/invalid operator usage by biasing generation toward syntactically and semantically validated building blocks.
minimal_test: Use GeoBench expressions to create an instruction-following variant of SR: for each GeoBench problem, generate 3 instruction conditions derived from the ground-truth form (operator-presence: must include sin or sqrt; structure: must be periodic or symmetric; and a negative constraint: must not include a specified operator). Compare two systems on the same open-weight LLM backbone: (A) instruction-only (ChatSR-style prompting) and (B) instruction + retrieval augmentation (RAG-SR-style): retrieve top-K expressions from the model's own search history for that instance (e.g., best-so-far by validation error) and include them in-context before generation. Keep search budget identical (same number of candidate evaluations) and run with K=0 vs K=5. Include an ablation diagnostic where retrieval is replaced by random previously evaluated expressions from other instances (to test whether gains are from grounding vs just extra tokens).
decisive_metric: Constraint satisfaction rate conditional on good fit: proportion of runs where the final expression (i) satisfies the instruction constraints exactly (operator present/absent and simple periodicity proxy via spectral peak or autocorrelation above threshold), and (ii) achieves within 5% of the best achievable MSE among candidates evaluated under the same budget. Report also the instruction-fit Pareto frontier (constraint satisfaction vs MSE) to detect anchoring tradeoffs. Diagnostic: change in constraint violations attributable to retrieved vs random retrieval.
supporting_result: Instruction + retrieval (K=5) improves constraint satisfaction-at-good-fit by a meaningful margin (e.g., +15-30 percentage points over K=0) while keeping median MSE within a small tolerance (e.g., <=5% relative increase), and random retrieval does not produce the same improvement, indicating the effect comes from grounding in relevant searched expressions rather than added context length.
falsifying_result: Retrieval augmentation fails to improve constraint satisfaction-at-good-fit versus instruction-only (difference near 0 or negative), or it improves constraint satisfaction only by significantly worsening fit (e.g., >15% relative MSE increase), or random retrieval matches the gains, implying retrieval grounding is not the mechanism and the direction is not worth pursuing for controllable SR under these constraints.

literature_gap: Delving Deep into Sim2Real proposes a distribution-gap metric (normalized sum of Mahalanobis distances) to guide synthetic-data integration, but its generality is questioned. WinSyn provides controllable synthetic-to-real factors (render/material/geometry) and semantic labels, yet does not validate whether a distribution-gap metric actually predicts downstream synthetic-to-real segmentation transfer under controlled domain shifts. This creates a cross-paper tension: does reducing the Mahalanobis-based distribution gap reliably translate into improved task performance on real data, or can it be gamed/misaligned with the real-task decision boundary?
hypothesis: If we select or transform WinSyn synthetic images to minimize the Mahalanobis-based distribution gap to the real WinSyn photos, real-image segmentation performance should increase because the selected synthetic subset better matches the real feature distribution relevant to the model.
minimal_test: Use WinSyn (synthetic pool + real photos with semantic labels). Train the same segmentation architecture (e.g., DeepLabV3-ResNet50 or SegFormer-B0 pretrained on ImageNet) under two synthetic-pretraining conditions before fine-tuning on a fixed small labeled real set (e.g., 500 labeled real crops): (A) synthetic subset chosen to minimize the Sim2Real Mahalanobis distribution-gap metric to the real unlabeled photo set (compute features using a fixed public encoder such as DINOv2-base or CLIP ViT-B/16); (B) size-matched random synthetic subset (WinSyn baseline). Keep synthetic subset size fixed (e.g., 10k images) and fine-tuning schedule identical. Include one ablation diagnostic: repeat (A) but compute Mahalanobis in two different feature spaces (DINOv2 vs CLIP) to see if conclusions depend on the representation used for the gap. Total compute fits in <=8 A100 GPU-days with small models and moderate image resolution crops.
decisive_metric: Mechanism check: correlation across multiple subset draws between (i) Mahalanobis distribution gap (per chosen subset) and (ii) improvement in real-domain mean IoU after fine-tuning (delta mIoU vs training with no synthetic). Report Spearman correlation and the slope of delta mIoU vs gap; also report whether the min-gap subset (A) beats random (B) in mIoU at equal synthetic-data budget.
supporting_result: Across at least 5 different subset draws/budgets, lower Mahalanobis gap consistently predicts higher real mIoU (significant negative Spearman correlation, e.g., rho <= -0.6), and the min-gap selection (A) yields a clear mIoU gain over random (B) at the same synthetic budget (e.g., +1 to +3 mIoU), with similar trends under both DINOv2- and CLIP-based gap computation.
falsifying_result: Mahalanobis gap shows weak or no relationship with real mIoU (e.g., |rho| < 0.2), and/or the min-gap subset (A) does not outperform random (B) (difference near zero or negative) despite achieving substantially lower measured gap; additionally, results flip depending on whether DINOv2 or CLIP features are used (indicating the metric is not a stable, task-relevant mechanism).

literature_gap: DIVA claims diffusion-based image-only feedback fixes CLIP’s fine-grained visual shortcomings that stem from biased/insufficiently distinctive text-image pairs, while Demystifying CLIP Data (MetaCLIP) argues CLIP performance is primarily a data curation issue. It is unclear whether DIVA’s gains are a genuinely new signal beyond what better-curated CLIP pretraining already provides, or whether DIVA mainly compensates for undertrained/under-curated CLIP variants. This cross-paper tension is untested because DIVA is not evaluated as a post-train on a data-curated CLIP (MetaCLIP) under controlled compute, nor disentangled from the “just train longer” explanation (Undertrained CLIP).
hypothesis: If DIVA’s diffusion feedback provides a distinct visual signal (not just compensating for poor data or insufficient training), then applying the same DIVA post-training to a MetaCLIP-initialized model should still yield measurable gains on fine-grained visual perception (e.g., orientation/quantity/color) beyond what is achievable by a compute-matched “resume training longer” baseline, because diffusion feedback injects visual distinctiveness not present in language metadata balancing or extra contrastive steps.
minimal_test: Use open weights: start from an available MetaCLIP ViT-B checkpoint (or closest open MetaCLIP variant) and an open CLIP ViT-B checkpoint. For each start point, run two compute-matched post-training variants for the same number of steps and batch size (total <=8 A100 GPU-days): (A) DIVA-style diffusion feedback post-training using image-only feedback as in Diffusion Feedback Helps CLIP See Better, and (B) a simple continued CLIP contrastive training baseline (resume training with the higher-LR heuristic from Your CLIP Model Might Be Undertrained, using a public image-text dataset like CC3M subset or LAION-400M subset if feasible; otherwise CC3M/CC12M). Evaluate all four resulting models on MMVP-VLM (or the publicly available fine-grained visual benchmark used by DIVA) and include a focused diagnostic subset targeting color/orientation/quantity prompts. Ablation/failure-mode diagnostic: run DIVA with diffusion feedback disabled (i.e., same pipeline but no diffusion guidance term, equivalent to doing nothing beyond normalization) to ensure gains are not from incidental training effects.
decisive_metric: Fine-grained perception accuracy delta on the targeted attributes (orientation, color, quantity, spatial relations) measured as per-MMVP-VLM subcategory accuracy (or attribute-specific accuracy on the diagnostic subset), reported as improvement over each model’s own pre-post baseline. The decisive comparison is: (MetaCLIP + DIVA) gain minus (MetaCLIP + continued-CLIP-training) gain, and whether this remains positive and non-trivial across the attribute categories.
supporting_result: On MetaCLIP initialization, DIVA yields consistent gains on multiple fine-grained subcategories (e.g., >=2 percentage points average improvement on the attribute-focused slice, with gains in at least 3 of 4 categories), and these gains exceed the compute-matched continued-training baseline by a clear margin (e.g., >=1 percentage point net advantage), while the diffusion-disabled ablation shows near-zero gain. This indicates diffusion feedback adds a distinct signal beyond better data curation and just training longer.
falsifying_result: On MetaCLIP initialization, DIVA provides no meaningful improvement over compute-matched continued training (e.g., net advantage <=0.3 percentage points or negative on the attribute-focused slice), or gains appear only on one category while degrading others, and/or the diffusion-disabled ablation performs similarly to DIVA. This would suggest DIVA mainly compensates for undertraining/under-curation rather than adding a distinct mechanism worth pursuing.

literature_gap: FedSRC claims privacy-preserving client self-regulation by having clients decide participation via local evaluation of the current global model (requires honest reporting), while HiCS-FL improves non-IID training via server-side heterogeneity estimation from client updates (potentially enabling client profiling). There is an unresolved cross-paper tension: can a lightweight, privacy-friendly proxy for client usefulness (FedSRC-style self-check) match the convergence/variance benefits of heterogeneity-guided sampling (HiCS-FL) without requiring server-side heterogeneity inference, and how fragile is each method to mild client misreporting/strategic behavior?
hypothesis: If we replace HiCS-FL's server-side heterogeneity score with a FedSRC-style client-side usefulness score (delta in local loss on a small public validation set between pre- and post-local-train, reported as a scalar), then convergence speed and training stability should remain close to HiCS-FL because both are selecting clients whose updates are most informative, but privacy leakage (ability to infer client heterogeneity) should drop because the server observes only a single coarse scalar rather than output-layer update structure.
minimal_test: Run 3-way FL comparison on a standard public non-IID benchmark with open models: CIFAR-10 with Dirichlet alpha=0.1 partition across 100 clients, 10 clients sampled per round, ResNet-18. Methods: (A) HiCS-FL as described (baseline from paper), (B) FedAvg uniform sampling, (C) Scalar-SRC sampling: each participating client computes s = loss_global(public_val) - loss_local_after_training(public_val) using a fixed small public validation set (e.g., 5k CIFAR-10 images held by server and downloadable by all clients), sends s to server; server selects next round clients by sampling proportionally to s (clipped at 0) among available clients. Failure-mode/ablation diagnostic: introduce 20% strategic clients that inflate their reported s by a constant factor (e.g., +0.2) without changing their model update; evaluate robustness. Keep total compute within budget by limiting to 200 rounds, 1 local epoch, SGD, and 3 random seeds.
decisive_metric: Mechanism-matched diagnostics (not just final accuracy): (1) Update informativeness: per-round cosine similarity between aggregated update and full-participation FedAvg update computed on the same round (simulate full participation once every 10 rounds to estimate the 'ideal' direction). (2) Privacy/profiling risk proxy: train a simple classifier at server to predict each client's dominant class (or entropy of label distribution) using only the observed selection signal (HiCS-FL: output-layer update features; Scalar-SRC: scalar s history); report AUC/accuracy. (3) Robustness: change in (1) and in convergence variance when 20% clients misreport s.
supporting_result: Scalar-SRC achieves similar update-direction alignment to HiCS-FL (e.g., within 5-10% relative gap in cosine similarity to the full-participation direction across rounds) and similar or lower training variance than FedAvg, while server-side heterogeneity inference is significantly harder (profiling classifier near chance for Scalar-SRC but substantially above chance for HiCS-FL). Under 20% misreporting, Scalar-SRC degrades gracefully (small drop in alignment/variance), indicating practical robustness comparable to HiCS-FL.
falsifying_result: Scalar-SRC shows materially worse update-direction alignment than HiCS-FL (e.g., >20% relative drop sustained over training) and/or substantially higher training variance, indicating the scalar usefulness signal is insufficient to capture heterogeneity-driven informativeness; or the profiling classifier remains highly predictive under Scalar-SRC (similar to HiCS-FL), indicating no privacy advantage; or mild misreporting causes large instability (sharp drop in alignment and spiking variance), undermining the self-regulation premise.

literature_gap: STARC proposes reward-function distance metrics with tight regret bounds, while the error-regret mismatch work shows low reward-model error can still yield high regret under distribution shift during optimization. It is unclear whether a reward-distance metric like STARC is actually predictive of error-regret mismatch in practical learned-reward settings (e.g., preference-learned interpretable rewards via DDTs), or whether small metric distance can still coincide with large realized regret after policy optimization.
hypothesis: If STARC distance to the ground-truth reward is a useful proxy for robustness to error-regret mismatch, then reward models with smaller STARC distance (even if both have similarly low preference training error) should induce smaller regret and less distribution-shift amplification during policy optimization, because STARC upper/lower bounds relate reward discrepancies to worst-case regret.
minimal_test: In a small, fully-specified environment with known true reward (e.g., CartPole from the DDT paper’s domain, or a small visual gridworld), generate preference data from an oracle (true-reward-induced comparisons). Train two reward models on the same preference dataset: (1) Differentiable Decision Tree reward model as in 'Can Differentiable Decision Trees Learn Interpretable Reward Functions?' and (2) an MLP reward model baseline (as that paper compares against). Ensure both achieve matched held-out preference accuracy (by tuning capacity/regularization). For each trained reward model, compute STARC distance to the known true reward (using the STARC framework). Then, for each learned reward, run the same RL optimizer to train a policy on the learned reward from the same initial state distribution. Evaluate each resulting policy’s regret under the true reward. Include an ablation diagnostic: repeat with policy regularization on/off (as discussed in the error-regret mismatch paper) to see whether any STARC-regret relationship is stable to regularization.
decisive_metric: Primary: rank-correlation across trained reward models/seeds between STARC distance to true reward and realized true-reward regret of the optimized policy (plus the slope of a simple linear fit: regret vs STARC). Diagnostic failure-mode: cases where two rewards have near-equal held-out preference error but substantially different regret; quantify whether STARC distinguishes these cases (difference in STARC vs difference in regret).
supporting_result: Across multiple random seeds (and optionally multiple preference dataset sizes), lower STARC distance consistently corresponds to lower true-reward regret after optimization (significant positive slope and high rank-correlation), and in matched-preference-error pairs, the lower-STARC model almost always yields lower regret. This relationship persists (same direction) with and without policy regularization.
falsifying_result: STARC distance shows near-zero or inconsistent correlation with realized regret (e.g., rank-correlation around 0, or frequent inversions where the lower-STARC reward yields higher regret), especially in the matched-preference-error comparisons; or policy regularization flips or destroys any apparent STARC-regret relationship. This would suggest STARC distance is not a practically decisive diagnostic for error-regret mismatch in learned-reward optimization.
